title: Understanding Transfer Learning of RNA Foundation Models on Downstream Tasks
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Pretraining helps only when aligned with the task: fine-tuning usually beats random initialization and frozen features, which often fail.
layout: 3x3 grid of grouped bar charts, shared legend on top, dashed baselines
description: A 3x3 grid of grouped bar charts, one per RNA downstream task, labeled (a) to (i). The tasks are Archive2, bpRNA, SSI, MRL, ncRNA, mRNA, mRNA-ood, Ribozyme and Ribozyme-ood. A single legend runs along the top. Each chart has nine models on the x-axis, from RNA-BERT through OmniGenome-186M to mRNA-FM, with rotated labels. Every model has three hatched bars: orange for pretrained fine-tuning, crimson for random-init training, and dark purple for frozen linear probing. A red dashed horizontal line marks the one-hot baseline. A black dash-dot line marks prior SOTA on the first five panels. Arrows in the titles show whether higher or lower is better. The eye goes first to the tall orange bars that clear the baselines. Panels where the purple bars are low show that frozen features do not transfer.
caption: For each task, the orange bars (PT-FT) represent the performance of RNA foundation models fine-tuned from pretrained weights, while the red bars (RI-T) correspond to models trained from random initialization on downstream tasks. The purple bars (Frozen) denote performance obtained by applying linear probing to frozen last-layer representations of pretrained RNA foundation models. The red dashed lines indicate results achieved using one-hot sequence representations (Onehot), and the black dash–dot lines represent previously reported state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance. Across most tasks, fine-tuning from pretrained weights consistently outperforms the Onehot baseline. In particular, models such as OmniGenome-52M and OmniGenome-186M achieve performance that is consistently superior to, or at least comparable with, the reported SOTA results across all nine evaluated tasks.
abstract: Foundation models (FMs) pretrained on large-scale sequence data have emerged as a promising paradigm for RNA biology, yet the mechanisms underlying their transferability remain unclear. In this work, we conduct a systematic investigation of transfer learning in RNA FMs across diverse structural and functional tasks. Our results demonstrate that frozen representations from pretrained RNA FMs are not universally transferable, and that the hierarchical feature reuse paradigm prevalent in computer vision does not generally extend to RNA FMs. Instead, pretraining primarily benefits downstream tasks by providing a favorable optimization initialization when pretraining and downstream objectives are well aligned, which accelerates convergence toward flatter minima associated with improved generalization. Overall, our findings characterize pretraining as an optimization prior whose effectiveness is governed by task alignment and model capacity, offering principled guidance for future RNA FMs.
